en: Of the extraordinary Lady Chürök,
The calamity on everyone’s lips,
They said: “She has a thimble mouth and camel-calf eyes,
And speech as sweet as honey and sugar.
Above her lip
There is the faintest trace
Of a tiny beauty mark.
May your sister-in-law’s suffering end—
Where is any flaw in her?
She has the finest long hair;
The noble, ill-fated woman
Is the mightiest among women.
Look upon Chürök’s beauty—
The purest wearer of a flowing dress;
Is this not the very beauty,
The queen of all women?”
That day warrior Kyyaz
Stirred the people and held his feast,
Carrying out a plan no man could conceive.
“Kyyaz has taken Chürök,” they said;
Of all men anyone had seen,
“Warrior Kyyaz has become the gray-maned champion,” they said.
The people bustled, holding a feast,
And while the multitude stood thus,
Hero Kiyaz, son of Bagysh,
Who ruled the people and sustained the realm—
Was this not Khan Kiyaz?
He was a lord of highest rank;
Among the Zhediger of Jeti-Ozon,
The accomplished Kiyaz became khan.
Such was Kiyaz's standing.
Wrapped in the blue haze of celebration,
Such was Kiyaz when you saw him.
He strained like a gray tiger,
His weapons set in order;
Such was hero Kiyaz's bearing.
A bare sword hung at his side,
Like a cloud returning with rain,
Wrath spread across his face.
Thick-wristed and stone-hearted—
If you ask what Kiyaz was like,
He was powerfully built and fierce.
His lashes were flame, his eyes embers;
Among men there was none like him.
Looming over the front of his saddle,
Broad as a tinsmith's bellows,
His bristling mustache
Was like the handle of a great whip.
Above his eyes, his black brows
Were like fists turned downward.
This formidable Kiyaz—
Such was his appearance.
He towered, huge-limbed,
With anger as vast as a mountain.
When this Kiyaz grew enraged,
He seemed ready to swallow his opponent.
Then hero Kiyaz,
On the plain of Jeti-Ozon,
Having carried Churok off,
Was holding the feast for taking her.
"All the precious four kinds of livestock
I mean to scatter lavishly,"
Was Kiyaz's intention.
Dust flew into the sky;
The army seethed in a dusty throng.
Hero Kiyaz, son of Bagysh,
Had brought relentless turmoil,
The people said.
Moonlike Lady Churok,
Taken as spoil from Talas,
Akun's daughter Churok,
He had brought away, they said.
Her gold and silver
He had loaded and carried off, they said.
Moonlike Lady Churok—
After ravaging and destroying her camp,
He had seized her, they said.
"The lands of old Talas and great Keng-Kol
I have won and brought home;
For the fallen and extinguished Zhediger,
I have taken vengeance," he said.
"Upon the steed none would give when asked,
I cast the cruel catching-pole;
Churok, who would not consent in her right mind,
I have taken and led away as spoil.
Today I mean to scatter all four kinds of livestock
At the bride Churok's wedding.
My people, now that you have come, I shall spare nothing.
Zhediger of Jeti-Ozon,
Your khan stands here before you.
All you multitudes born into this world,
Every one of you stands here.
Say, 'This is Khan Kiyaz's design;
This is Aichurok's wedding.'
Let cries and clamor abound;
Let the din split the sky.
Let dust trail upward from the earth;
Let all these accomplished people rejoice.
I shall scatter livestock by the tens of thousands;
The treasury left by my father Bagysh—
I shall break open its mouth with an axe.
My people, let me slaughter the cattle;
For valiant Lady Churok,
Let me hold her wedding today.
Gather livestock from every quarter;
Let the wealth from my hands be spent.
Today perform my marriage rite with Churok.
Today we shall eat meat from one dish
And face each other in one bed.
Today I shall scatter all my livestock;
For the noble, unfortunate woman,
Today I shall spend all my poor means.
Upon the broad plain,
For this unfortunate woman's wedding,
My people, know this today:
I shall slaughter a thousand dark mares,
I shall slaughter a thousand blaze-faced camels.
Let the poles bend today;
Let champion warriors joust today!
Let poles break and lashings fall;
At renowned Churok's wedding,
Let heroes fall and lashings drop.
Let the strongest wrestlers come forward,
Wearing yellow leather trousers;
Let them seize each other by the cuffs,
Let them wrestle on foot,
And let the victor become rich.
Let no tale remain that she was a woman taken as spoil;
Let no such talk remain among the people.
Let no resentment remain that she was a plundered woman;
Let no such grudge remain within.
Let all the peoples think,
'It was as though he took a maiden in marriage.'
Let no other thought arise.
Let them say, 'Khan Kiyaz was a leopard warrior;
Such was his intention.
When he took Aichurok,
Such was the wedding he held.'
To all the gathered souls,
To children chasing butterflies,
To old men coughing often,
To the senile who cannot come to the feast,
To old men remaining at home,
Let them say, 'This was hero Kiyaz's desire;
Such was his intention.
The dear ruler of the people—
Such was the feast he held.'
Set aside excessive talk;
Take whatever you desire.
Hold fierce games and great wrestling;
My people, this is what I desire!"
So spoke hero Kiyaz.
Because of what had happened,
Because of Aichurok,
He gathered the people behind him;
Driven by his longing for Aichurok,
The multitude of Zhediger
Heard that the khan's decree had come.
The poles bent,
And champion warriors jousted.
Broken poles piled like a mountain;
They straightened their poles in their grip,
Thrusting them out at full length,
Boasting to one another,
And clashing fiercely in the joust.
When their poles met,
They shattered at the middle with a crack.
At the great feast held by Lord Kiyaz,
The multitude of Zhediger
Rejoiced and bustled.
Wrestlers fell, propping themselves up;
Men were thrown from their horses.
Those thrown and those who threw them
Stripped one another bare,
Plundering each other completely.
They seized each other by the trouser cuffs;
Heroes and wrestlers grappled,
Putting forth all their former strength.
They butted like gray bulls,
And fought like wolves in kok-boru.
They gripped whatever opening appeared;
The wrestlers, finding an opening,
Mauled each other like hungry stallion-camels.
Along Jeti-Ozon,
The people bustled and raised a din.
The one thrown was left empty-handed;
The victor claimed the prize.
The spectacle grew immense.
Dust flew into the sky;
The great crowd streamed and bustled.
Now, to begin the celebration,
To perform Churok's marriage rite,
Those with turbans wound around their heads,
Those who prayed to the Almighty,
The khojas in white turbans,
The mullahs in mottled robes—
He gathered every khoja without exception.
As twilight came and the sun set,
As darkness fell and people grew still,
When the sky filled with glittering stars,
When every living creature
Had reached its time for sleep,
He had the marriage rite performed at once,
And Kiyaz took Churok.
Caught in a net she could not break by struggling,
Aichurok had fallen into the snare.
She had fallen into hands
In a way no sleeping person could dream.
Conceiving a plan no person could discover,
Kiyaz, hero of the Zhediger,
Held a feast for all the accomplished people.
They called it hero Kiyaz's design,
The wedding at which he would take Aichurok.
He slaughtered ninety mares for the feast;
Abundant wealth and countless livestock
He set out without measure.
He seated all the champions facing the feast,
And made a mountain of meat like Ala-Too,
A lake of broth like Ala-Kol.
He filled the feast with slaughtered stock
And plunged into the clamor.
A great spectacle beyond human knowing
Had plunged into uproar;
A vast commotion that would not subside
Had engulfed them.
A spectacle that could not be stilled
Had plunged into clamor.
The people who came to the feast—
Some called for a stallion and mounted a camel;
The shameless went on foot.
All the women streamed along,
The old and the young;
Even the drunkards came, none staying behind.
The long-eared gossips,
All the modest people,
The eager connoisseur and the handsome,
The meek man who knew no speeches,
The khoja wrapped in a turban,
The lettered mullah,
The wrestlers and spearmen—
Hearing Kiyaz would take Churok,
They all came, none remaining behind.
They came to this feast,
People of every kind.
Drinking kumis, they grew heated,
Their bones tingling;
Drinking spirits, they panted,
Straining like hungry birds.
Kiyaz, son of Bagysh,
Showed himself to be a hero.
Many people rejoiced at his feast;
Great were the games and spectacle,
When one looked upon such events.
What could poor Kiyaz do?
Without looking up or down,
Never thinking he might die,
